title: Processes, descriptors, and signals
summary: Supervise worker processes with a bounded pool, private descriptors, signal forwarding, and checked exit codes.

scenario.briefing: The campus batch runner starts every job at once, loses track of its children when it exits, and reports success even when workers fail. Replace the naive loop with a supervisor that reads the job list on its own descriptor, keeps four workers running, forwards termination, and exits nonzero when any job fails.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: Keep a counter of running jobs and call wait -n before starting another when it reaches MAX_PARALLEL.
Open jobs.txt with exec 3< and read with read -r job_id <&3; close descriptor 3 for the worker with 3<&-.
Start run_job in the background, save $! in pids, and let the trap forward SIGTERM to each job.
Run wait -n until no jobs remain and set status=1 whenever a wait returns nonzero.

misconceptions.testDescription: The job list is read on a private descriptor and closed for workers.
misconceptions.feedback: Threads share the process address space, so a private descriptor per worker prevents accidental sharing of the job list.

misconceptions.description: Supervising without reaping children or checking exit status.
misconceptions.testDescription: Every child is reaped and any failure makes the supervisor exit nonzero.
misconceptions.feedback: Unreaped children become zombies, and a zero exit hides a failed job. Wait for every child and propagate failure.

misconceptions.description: Believing a process can catch SIGKILL.
misconceptions.feedback: SIGKILL is delivered by the kernel and cannot be caught, blocked, or handled. Use SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.

sections.title: Processes and threads
sections.body: A process owns a virtual address space, a file descriptor table, and at least one thread of execution. Threads in one process share that address space and those descriptors, so a bad write in one thread can corrupt another. Separate processes pay for isolation with memory and startup cost, which is why a batch runner can use one process per job and supervise them from a small parent.

sections.title: Virtual memory
sections.body: The kernel gives each process its own virtual address space and maps pages to physical frames through page tables. A pointer is an address in that private space, not a physical address, so two processes can use the same numeric address for different data. The mapping also lets the kernel leave pages on disk, share read-only pages, and kill one process with an out-of-memory error without touching its neighbors.

sections.title: Descriptors are per-process handles
sections.body: A file descriptor is a small integer indexing the process's descriptor table. 0, 1, and 2 are stdin, stdout, and stderr. A child inherits open descriptors across fork and exec, so a worker that inherits the job list can read it or keep the file open after the parent closes it. Open the list on descriptor 3, use it only for reading jobs, and close it in the child with 3<&-.

sections.title: Signals and exit codes
sections.body: A signal is an asynchronous notification. SIGTERM requests termination and can be caught, SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored, and SIGINT comes from the terminal. A shell reports a child killed by signal N as 128 + N, and wait returns the child's status to the parent that reaps it. Check every status: a supervisor that ignores wait reports success while its workers fail.

sections.title: Orphans, zombies, and bounded concurrency
sections.body: An orphan is a running process whose parent exited; it is reparented and keeps running. A zombie has exited but still holds a process table entry until its parent calls wait. A supervisor must reap children and bound how many run at once: starting every job at once exhausts memory and descriptors, and wait -n gives a simple slot-based limit.

vocabulary.definition: A running program with its own virtual address space, descriptor table, and at least one thread.
An execution context inside a process that shares the process's address space and descriptors.
The private set of addresses the kernel presents to one process and maps to physical memory.
A small per-process integer that names an open file, pipe, or socket.
An asynchronous notification delivered to a process, such as SIGTERM or SIGINT.
An exited process whose status has not been collected by its parent.
A process whose parent exited, leaving it reparented to another process.
The status a process returns to its parent, where zero means success.

steps.title: Write a bounded worker supervisor
steps.prompt: Edit processes.md. Replace the naive loop with a supervisor that bounds concurrency to four workers, reads jobs on descriptor 3, closes that descriptor for each worker, forwards SIGTERM and SIGINT, and exits nonzero if any worker fails. Keep the explanation of processes, descriptors, signals, and exit codes accurate.

files.content:
# Worker supervisor

The script runs each job in jobs.txt and writes one log per job.

~~~bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

JOBS_FILE="jobs.txt"
LOG_DIR="logs"
MAX_PARALLEL=4

mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"

# TODO: bound concurrency, isolate the job list, forward signals, and check exit codes
for job_id in $(cat "$JOBS_FILE"); do
    ./worker.sh "$job_id" >"$LOG_DIR/$job_id.log" 2>&1 &
done

echo "all jobs started"
~~~

## Process model

Each worker is a separate process. The supervisor does not wait for them.

tests.description: The loop keeps at most four jobs running.
The job list is read on a private descriptor and closed for workers.
Each worker gets a deadline and no inherited job list.
Termination is forwarded to every running job.
Every child is reaped and any failure makes the supervisor exit nonzero.

hints: Bound how many workers can run at once.
Give each worker only the descriptors it needs.
Forward termination and set a deadline for every child.
Reap every child, close inherited descriptors, and exit nonzero if any job fails.

steps.title: Process and signal semantics

statements.label: Threads in one process share its address space, while separate processes do not.
A virtual address is the same as the physical address of the memory it maps.
A file descriptor is a per-process index into a table of open files.
SIGKILL can be caught so a process can clean up before exiting.
A zombie has exited but remains in the process table until its parent reaps it.
An orphan is a child that exited while its parent still runs.

steps.explanation: A process is the isolation boundary: it gets its own virtual address space and descriptor table, while threads share both inside it. Descriptors are per-process handles inherited across fork and exec, so a private descriptor must be closed for children. SIGTERM is a catchable request, SIGKILL is not, and the exit status a parent reaps is how it learns that a child failed.
hints: Threads share an address space; processes do not.
A descriptor is a handle into the process's table.
SIGKILL cannot be caught or cleaned up.
Select process/thread, descriptors, and zombies; reject virtual-address and SIGKILL claims.
